title: From Pilot to Production: Why Banking AI Projects Stall and How To Ensure Success
excerpt: . Despite $30 to $40 billion of enterprise investment into generative artificial intelligence, a Massachusetts Institute of Technology report revealed that 95% of organizations are getting zero return. Since the report’s release last year, this statistic has been referred to constantly when discussing AI’s potential. Daragh Morrissey, global AI lead for financial services at Microsoft , says whether or not the stat is true to the experience of most financial services institutions, it’s not necessarily a bad thing. BizTech spoke with him about how financial organizations are faring with scaling their AI initiatives and what they can do to ensure success as their approach to AI shifts from pilots to launching enterprisewide applications. DISCOVER: This is a new era of digital banking powered by AI technology. BIZTECH: The statistic that 95% of generative AI pilots fail is commonly referred to. Does it sound right, based on your experience?. MORRISSEY: What we’re seeing is a period of rapid learning and iteration across the industry. Many pilots are achieving strong technical results and delivering value at the team or individual level, even if they haven’t yet been fully operationalized at scale. What Microsoft is seeing with customers is an incredibly positive impact. Look at how many CEOs are talking about it in their earnings reports, for example. I recently heard a CIO address that statistic directly, and his perspective really stuck with me. He pointed out that the number itself is less concerning today because the cost and speed of experimentation have changed so dramatically. A few years ago, building a proof of concept could take months and significant investment, so a high failure rate was far more consequential. Today, teams can stand up and iterate on ideas in a matter of hours, not months, often taking something from concept to production-ready in a fraction of the time. So, in many ways, what’s being framed as “failure” is actually a natural and necessary part of rapid experimentation at scale. That said, organizations are quickly moving beyond experimentation and starting to understand what it takes to embed AI into real business workflows and drive measurable outcomes. The focus now is shifting toward scaling what works, and we’re already seeing a growing set of institutions doing that successfully. So, rather than focusing on the percentage that hasn’t been scaled yet, I think the more important takeaway is how quickly the industry is learning, and how rapidly those early successes are being translated into broader transformation. Click the banner below to power employee productivity with AI. BIZTECH: What are the obstacles that lead to AI initiative failures in the finance sector? How much of the problem is technology, and how much is organizational readiness?. MORRISSEY: In financial services, the barriers are much more organizational than technological. The technology is maturing rapidly, but many institutions still face fundamental challenges with data, process and skills. Common obstacles include fragmented or poorly governed data , integration challenges with legacy systems , difficulty measuring return on investment and a shortage of AI-specific skills. There is also often a disconnect between AI teams and business stakeholders, which makes it harder to embed solutions into real workflows. The banks driving impact have the CEO as the chief AI officer. They lead from the top, and I’ve seen incredible collaboration inside the organizations. AI is helping bridge the gap between IT and business teams, fostering stronger collaboration and a more unified focus on delivering impact. Related Content:. title: HSBC plans to cut up to 70% of adviser roles as AI reshapes wealth management
excerpt: Strategic HR. HSBC plans to cut up to 70% of adviser roles as AI reshapes wealth management. Samriddhi Srivastava •. | 8 October 2026. HSBC is reportedly preparing deep workforce reductions across its UK wealth management division as the bank accelerates AI adoption and expands digitally enabled customer services. AI is increasingly reshaping workforce strategies in global banking, with HSBC reportedly planning significant job cuts across its UK wealth management business. According to a report by the Financial Times, cited by Reuters, HSBC is considering sweeping reductions across management, specialist and adviser roles as part of a broader effort to integrate artificial intelligence into its operations. The proposed restructuring highlights a growing trend across the financial services sector, where banks are investing heavily in AI-driven efficiencies while reassessing traditional workforce models. Wealth management workforce faces major restructuring. The Financial Times reported that HSBC plans to reduce approximately half of management and specialist positions within its UK wealth management business. The report further stated that cuts affecting financial advisers could reach as high as 70% , making it one of the most significant workforce restructuring efforts within the division. While HSBC does not publicly disclose employee numbers for its UK wealth management unit, the Financial Times noted that the business is believed to employ hundreds of relationship managers across the country. Key reported workforce changes include:. • Up to 70% reduction in financial adviser roles • Around 50% reduction in management and specialist positions • Workforce changes linked to broader AI integration efforts • Employees reportedly expected to exit by the end of the month following consultation processes. Digital transformation moves to the centre of strategy. In a statement quoted by Reuters, HSBC UK said it continues to evolve its services through more digitally enabled products and customer journeys to meet changing client expectations. The reported workforce reductions come as Georges Elhedery , HSBC's chief executive officer, pushes a strategy centred on technology simplification, automation and artificial intelligence. Since assuming the top role in 2024, Elhedery has positioned AI as a core component of HSBC's future operating model, deploying the technology across multiple functions and business units. Executive warnings on AI and employment. The latest developments follow comments made by Elhedery during HSBC's investor day event in May. According to Reuters, the chief executive told employees to embrace AI-driven transformation and acknowledged that generative AI would eliminate certain jobs while creating new opportunities elsewhere. His remarks reflected a wider debate unfolding across industries as organisations evaluate how automation and AI can improve productivity while altering workforce requirements. Banking sector enters a new phase of AI adoption. HSBC's reported plans come amid accelerating AI investments across global banking and financial services institutions. Banks are increasingly using AI to support customer service, wealth management, risk assessment, compliance and operational processes. As adoption expands, organisations are reviewing role structures, workforce composition and future skills requirements. For employers and HR leaders, the developments offer another indication of how AI is moving beyond experimentation and becoming a key driver of organisational redesign. Topics. # Layoffs. Author. title: AI Can Explain Why Your Loan Was Denied, Can The Bank Prove It? – OpEd
excerpt: . Opinion 1 Business Technology. October 12, 2026 October 12, 2026 Burak Oktenli 0 Comments. By Burak Oktenli. Facebook Twitter Email Flipboard Mastodon LinkedIn Share. Key Takeaways:. Generative AI risks making credit-denial notices more convincing yet detached from the actual multi-stage decision, so that a letter may cite a model’s top risk factors while the real refusal stemmed from an affordability rule or disputed debt. U. S. Regulation B still requires adverse-action notices to identify the principal reasons the creditor actually considered; recent supervisory adjustments and lighter CFPB examinations do not remove that obligation or the lender’s responsibility for vendor-supplied scores. The remedy is a preserved “decision trace” of inputs, model versions, policy rules and overrides, allowing notice-writing AI only to translate approved reasons, with practical tests that confirm the letter remains accurate after corrections or system updates. As new credit models learn from spending and cash-flow patterns, the challenge is no longer producing an explanation. It is proving that the explanation belongs to the decision that was made. Imagine a borrower receiving a carefully written rejection letter. The bank says she has not lived at her address long enough. She has been there seven years. An unrelated debt, mistakenly attached to her file, actually prevented approval. The automated notice is courteous, specific and wrong. This case is hypothetical. The vulnerability it illustrates is real: in a lending process assembled from data providers, risk scores, internal rules and human judgment, a plausible explanation can become detached from the decision it is supposed to describe. Generative AI could make that mistake more convincing rather than more obvious. That question has become particularly timely. On October 6, financial technology company Plaid introduced new cash-flow-based lending models , including LendScore Arc, which examines the sequence and timing of financial transactions. The company says its system converts model contributions into understandable reason codes, and it describes a method for tracing those contributions back to transactions. Those are constructive attempts to address a hard technical problem, not evidence that the product has generated inaccurate notices. But they also make the next question unavoidable. If a lender takes a reason code from one model, combines its score with another vendor’s information, applies an internal policy and perhaps permits a human override, what exactly explains the final refusal?. A reason for a score is not always a reason for a denial. A modern credit decision can have several stages. A third party estimates repayment risk. The lender checks affordability, verifies identity, applies eligibility rules and decides whether an exception is permitted. A separate service may generate the letter. Each stage can be legitimate. Confusion begins when the letter explains the wrong one. Suppose an applicant passes the model’s credit-risk threshold but fails an affordability rule based on a disputed obligation. A notice assembled from the model’s top-ranked risk factors could sound technically sophisticated while omitting the reason the lender actually declined the application. Reversing the sequence can produce the same error: a bank might report an internal rule that played no part in a rejection already determined by an earlier score. The problem is not that machine learning cannot contribute to creditworthiness assessments. Richer financial data may help lenders recognize applicants whose limited credit histories fail to capture steady income or responsible cash management. The problem arises when a system that predicts risk is mistaken for a complete record of how an institution exercised its decision authority. title: Woori Bank deploys AI fraud system and hires ex-police expert in Korea - CHOSUNBIZ
excerpt: By Song Ki-young. Published 2026. 10. 12. 17:17. Prefer Chosunbiz EN on Google. Woori Bank will launch a new system to block financial fraud by combining Generative AI and telecommunications information. Woori Bank also hired a former police investigative expert who led the arrest of a voice phishing ring leader. Woori Bank said it will strengthen its financial fraud prevention system centered on a dedicated unit, former police specialists, and the fraudulent transaction detection system (FDS), after holding a "financial fraud prevention press briefing" at its headquarters in Jung District, Seoul, on the 12th. It plans to build a next-generation detection framework using Generative AI and telecommunications data and expand information sharing with financial and investigative authorities. Jeong Jin-wan, Woori Bank president, said, "Because preventing financial fraud is about protecting not only customers' asset but also trust in finance, we are pursuing it as a top management priority," adding, "Once damage occurs, it is already too late. We will go a step beyond post-relief to identify risks early and preemptively block them before harm occurs. ". Woori Bank will operate a new AI monitoring system next month and work to stabilize it by year-end. While the existing FDS detected anomalies based on preset rules and financial transaction information, the bank plans to use Generative AI to analyze new financial fraud schemes and suspicious transaction patterns to boost detection capabilities. It is also pushing to build a next-generation FDS that links not only financial transaction data such as account transfers, deposits and withdrawals, card payments, and overseas remittances, but also electronic finance FDS, login records, and product usage information. The aim is to more broadly analyze anomalies in financial transactions and supplement the limits of the current detection system. Woori Bank has hired a former police investigative expert and created a department dedicated to preventing financial fraud. Jeon Jae-hong, the head senior manager of the financial fraud prevention department, the first such hire in the banking sector, is a financial fraud investigation expert who worked in the police for 24 years and retired as a senior superintendent. Jeon led the arrests of executives including the ringleader of the first-generation voice phishing ring "Head of Team Kim Mi-young," and investigations into overseas voice phishing rings. Jeon said, "In the past, a single ring committed crimes mainly by phone, but recently the development of technology, luring victims and executing crimes, and moving and laundering funds have each become specialized," adding, "As AI-driven financial fraud is expected to gain more ground, we have no choice but to respond with AI. ". Woori Bank said it is also achieving results in preventing damage using the existing FDS. From April to August this year, it forwarded 639 pieces of information suspected of money laundering from the FDS to the anti-money laundering (AML) department, of which 83 led to suspicious transaction reports (STR) after further analysis. During the same period, it also shared with the financial sector, through the AI platform for sharing and analyzing voice phishing information (ASAP), information on 664 suspicious accounts at other banks. Jeon said, "We expect AI to perform in a short time tasks that are difficult for people to handle one by one or that take a long time," adding, "We will strengthen the responsibility and expertise of the dedicated department to become a bank that leads in preventing financial fraud. title: How Artificial Intelligence Is Transforming Banking and Financial Services in India
excerpt: . Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how banks detect fraud, assess loan applications and serve customers. From answering routine banking queries to helping financial institutions identify suspicious transactions, AI is becoming an important part of modern financial services. In India, the expansion of digital payments, mobile banking and fintech platforms has created new opportunities for AI-driven services. The technology could help banks operate more efficiently, reach underserved customers and make financial services more accessible. However, its success will depend on how effectively institutions address data privacy, cybersecurity, fairness and customer trust. AI Is Making Banking More Convenient. Customers increasingly expect banking services to be available whenever they need them. AI-powered chatbots and virtual assistants help meet this demand by answering common questions, guiding users through banking processes and providing assistance outside regular branch hours. These tools can handle routine enquiries about transactions, account services and payment procedures, allowing customer service teams to focus on more complicated issues. AI can also help banks identify customer preferences and offer relevant financial information. For example, a banking application could analyse spending patterns to help a customer understand monthly expenses or plan savings. Such services must be based on appropriate consent and clear data-protection practices. Smarter Fraud Detection and Cybersecurity. As more people use digital payments, financial institutions face growing pressure to identify suspicious activity quickly. Traditional security systems often rely on predefined rules, while AI can analyse larger volumes of transactions and identify patterns that may indicate unusual behaviour. An AI-powered system might flag a sudden change in spending, repeated payment attempts or transactions that differ significantly from a customer’s usual activity. The bank can then request additional verification or investigate the alert. AI is also being explored as a tool for identifying emerging cyber threats and helping security teams prioritise potential incidents. Nevertheless, it is not a complete solution. Fraudsters can change their methods, and automated systems may sometimes flag legitimate payments incorrectly. Strong authentication, regular system testing and human investigation remain essential. AI Could Improve Access to Credit. Loan applications often require lenders to assess income, repayment capacity, existing liabilities and credit history. AI can help organise this information and support faster, more consistent credit assessments. The potential benefits extend beyond established borrowers. Small businesses and individuals with limited conventional credit histories may have difficulty obtaining loans, even when they have the capacity to repay them. Where regulations permit, responsibly assessed alternative data may provide lenders with additional information to evaluate such applicants. The Press Information Bureau’s May 2026 backgrounder, AI-Powered Financial Inclusion in India , highlights the potential of digital public infrastructure and AI to support more accessible financial services, including lending to micro, small and medium enterprises. However, faster decisions are not necessarily fairer decisions. Models trained on biased or incomplete data can reproduce existing inequalities. Banks must test their systems for bias, explain important decisions in understandable language and provide appropriate channels for customers to challenge errors. Automating Routine Banking Operations. A considerable amount of banking work involves processing forms, checking documents, reviewing records and responding to repetitive enquiries. title: Emirates NBD Launches AI Travel Assistant with Visa and Tripadvisor
excerpt: Emirates NBD has launched what it describes as the UAE’s first bank-led AI Travel Assistant, built in partnership with Visa and Tripadvisor. The conversational tool is accessible without a bank account or login, available free via the Emirates NBD website and a dedicated Tripadvisor domain, and is positioned by the bank as part of a broader shift towards ecosystem-led digital banking. The platform lets users describe their preferences, budget and travel style in plain language, returning tailored itineraries, destination picks and local recommendations. It draws on Tripadvisor’s repository of more than one billion reviews and eight million listings, with what the partners describe as enhanced customisation across the 15 destinations most popular among UAE travellers. Relevant Visa cardholder perks, including hotel discounts and car rental offers, surface dynamically within the conversation. Rohit Garg , group head of retail products and chief digital officer of retail banking and wealth management at Emirates NBD, said: “By combining cutting-edge AI with world-class insights from our partners, we are empowering travellers with innovative and personalised digital experiences that simplifies the process for our customers around one of their biggest passion points. ”. Strategic context. The product is framed internally as a lifestyle extension rather than a transactional banking feature, reflecting a pattern seen across Gulf and South-East Asian retail banks where the battle for primary customer relationships is increasingly fought through non-financial engagement. Emirates NBD points to internal data showing the average UAE resident plans seven trips annually and can spend up to three months researching a single trip, an observation consistent with the broader fragmentation of the online travel market following the retreat of several all-in-one itinerary platforms. The open-access design, requiring neither an Emirates NBD account nor a Visa card to use the basic tool, is commercially notable. It widens the top of the acquisition funnel at the cost of diluting the product’s exclusivity as a cardholder benefit. The Visa offer integration provides a reason for cardholders to prefer it, but the underlying travel content is freely available to anyone, which limits lock-in. How Emirates NBD measures conversion from travel planning to card spend or account opening will be the real test of commercial viability. Market and competitive landscape. Several large retail banks and card networks have moved into AI-assisted travel planning over the past 18 months, typically by embedding large language model interfaces into existing reward or concierge products. Mastercard , American Express and a number of European neobanks have announced or deployed comparable features, making the “first bank-led” positioning primarily a regional rather than a global claim. The UAE’s digital banking environment, shaped by the Central Bank of the UAE ‘s open-finance roadmap and a high smartphone penetration rate, is a credible testbed for lifestyle banking products, and Emirates NBD’s scale across 13 countries and 25 million active customers gives it distribution leverage that smaller challengers lack. For Tripadvisor, the partnership represents a distribution deal as much as a product collaboration. The platform has faced sustained pressure from AI-native travel search tools and Google’s own integrated travel features; embedding its review graph inside a bank’s customer journey offers a defensible distribution channel outside the direct-to-consumer search funnel. The tool is available in English at launch. Expansion to Arabic, the primary language of a substantial share of the bank’s customer base, is an obvious next step that the release did not address, nor did it provide any adoption targets or metrics against which to judge the rollout’s success. title: Singapore Sets New AI Risk Rules for Finance. What They Mean for Brokers
excerpt: . Singapore Sets New AI Risk Rules for Finance. What They Mean for Brokers. 2 min read. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has drawn a clearer regulatory line around the use of artificial intelligence in financial services. On 7 October 2026, the regulator published its Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management, establishing supervisory expectations for financial institutions using AI, from traditional machine-learning models to Generative AI and increasingly autonomous AI agents. The guidelines follow a public consultation launched in November 2025 and will begin taking effect on 7 October 2027. AI is increasingly moving beyond chatbots and productivity tools into areas that can influence financial decisions, customer interactions, compliance, risk management and potentially execution itself. MAS specifically warns that AI agents with access to tools could autonomously perform erroneous or unauthorised actions. It also identifies financial, operational, conduct, financial crime and reputational risks arising from AI, alongside security, privacy and third-party risks associated particularly with Generative AI. A Framework Built Around Risk, Not a Ban on AI. The framework is not designed to slow the adoption of AI. Its central idea is proportionality. MAS expects financial institutions to understand where AI is being used, determine how important and risky each application is, and then apply controls that match that risk. A tool used to proofread an internal email clearly does not require the same controls as an AI model influencing investment recommendations or customer risk assessments. London's trading industry is coming home!. This distinction is important when considering whether the framework is "mandatory". These are guidelines setting out MAS' supervisory expectations, rather than a standalone piece of legislation imposing identical technical requirements on every company. Yet regulated firms should not interpret this as optional guidance. MAS states that all financial institutions should adhere to its high-level expectations when deploying AI, while implementation should be proportionate to their size, activities and AI risk exposure. The guidelines also complement existing MAS requirements and principles, including Fairness, Ethics, Accountability and Transparency, known as FEAT. MAS AI Guidelines:Implementation Timeline Date Requirements November2025 Public consultation launched 7 October2026 AI guidelines published 7 October2027 AI oversight, risk managementand policies 7 October2028 AI lifecycle controls,capabilities and infrastructure. This gives firms roughly one year to establish the core governance layer and another year to complete the broader operational framework. MAS has also said that it intends to consult the industry in 2027 on whether further guidance specifically addressing agentic AI would be useful. Who Needs to Follow the Guidelines?. The scope is broad. MAS says the guidelines apply to all financial institutions and all forms of AI technology. The categories listed by the regulator include banks, fund managers, financial advisers, insurers, payment institutions, exchanges, clearing houses, custodians, credit rating agencies and firms dealing in capital markets products. Exempt futures and OTC derivatives brokers are also explicitly included among the categories covered. Read full analysis on Finance Magnates Intelligence portal:. Economy Finance Magnates. title: In AI-era banking, trust has a new enforcer—the network
summary: From ATMs to AI agents, a bank's attack surface is expanding. See how the network closes the gap.
excerpt: An article from. Sponsored. In AI-era banking, trust has a new enforcer—the network. Published Oct. 12, 2026. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. Sponsored content. By Cisco. SPONSORED CONTENT BY. It's 2 a. m. and the branch is empty. There’s a lobby ATM humming quietly, a security camera blinking in the corner, and somewhere in the cloud, an AI agent is finishing a batch of overnight fraud scores. All of them are inside the bank's trust boundary, but each is managed as an isolated security problem. That fragmentation is no longer sustainable. Protecting every device, login, and autonomous script requires something different from standalone, bolted-on cybersecurity. Banks need one architecture with security and visibility built into every layer. Resilience comes from unifying tools, not adding more of them onto existing architectures. AI agents expand the unmanaged attack surface. Devices like ATMs, badge readers, and Internet of Things (IoT) devices lack the memory capacity and proper operating system (OS) to run powerful security features like endpoint detection and response (EDR) and host-based firewalls. It’s a vulnerability that banks have lived with for years. Now add the complexity of safeguarding AI agents, which access systems and execute application programming interface (API) calls without a human in the loop. Their "unlisted" entry points add new openings for attackers. It's no wonder 79% of financial services respondents say AI has already expanded their network's attack surface and 85% have already added security controls, specifically for AI workloads 1. That's encouraging, but adding more controls to an old architecture is like adding extra locks to a house with no foundation. It buys time, not resilience. Security fused into the network instead of bolted on. Routing all traffic through a centralized inspection appliance introduces latency that breaks apps like real-time fraud detection and creates single points of failure. In an industry where milliseconds separate a legitimate transaction from a blocked one, that delay is a major risk. A slow fraud check can mean a declined card or a fraudulent transfer that clears before it's flagged. Security fused into the network solves this. Protection is built directly into the switches. Traffic is checked and security enforced instantly, with the same safeguards, whether the request comes from a teller terminal, an ATM, or an AI agent. Action control plus access control. Traditionally, zero-trust security was focused on controlling access to the network. Now it must also control actions within the network perimeter. A security camera should connect and send data only to its recorder. An AI agent should read transaction history but be blocked from executing a fund transfer or accessing sensitive data, even if a hacker tricks it into misbehaving. For physical devices like ATMs and IoT sensors, action control relies on microsegmentation: isolating zones so each device can only reach what it’s allowed. For AI agents, enforcement must be at an even more granular level, governing individual API calls and tool requests so permissions are tied to specific actions instead of broad system access. Verified trust for compliance. Banking executives struggle to prove their AI and IoT environments are compliant with regulatory mandates because these systems are largely invisible to traditional monitoring. ATMs and IoT devices can't run endpoint agents. AI agents act autonomously with no port, no agent, and no asset tag to track. Regulations now demand continuous, real-time proof of resilience, but fragmented tools make it hard to produce one unified record of what happened and whether it was authorized. Integrating network telemetry with security operations fused into the network closes that gap. Every action is logged in real time against policy, creating a defensible, continuous audit trail. title: Superbank looks beyond credit scores with AI
excerpt: 1 day ago. 173 views. Melisa Hendrawati, chief financial officer at Superbank. Superbank looks beyond credit scores with AI. The bank monitors its lending models for bias and performance. PT Super Bank Indonesia is using artificial intelligence (AI) and customer behaviour data to assess borrowers overlooked by conventional credit scoring, letting it develop lending products for underserved segments whilst managing risk. “AI and analytics can help us analyze a broader range of customer and behavioral data to identify patterns that may not be captured through traditional credit assessment approaches,” Melisa Hendrawati, chief financial officer at Superbank, told Asian Banking & Finance. Join Asian Banking & Finance community. Indonesia’s third-biggest digital bank by assets uses those findings to group borrowers by risk, design credit products, set lending conditions, and adjust its credit strategy. Hendrawati said Superbank tests lending assumptions, monitors customer behaviour, and uses the results to refine products, shortening development time whilst improving its assessment of borrowers. AI does not replace human judgement in credit decisions, she said. The bank continues to monitor its models for bias and performance, ensuring they comply with regulatory requirements and its lending risk limits. Superbank also requires every AI project to have a defined business objective and measurable targets before approval. “Organisations must know the business outcome they want out of AI, otherwise it's just a good buzzword,” Hendrawati said in an emailed reply to questions. The bank first identifies the customer or operational problem a proposed tool will address, then tests it through pilot projects. Wider deployment depends on whether it meets predetermined performance targets. For lending, Superbank measures AI's contribution through better credit risk assessment, faster product development, and its ability to serve customers who are difficult to assess using conventional models. The bank also considers operating costs, customer engagement, and employee productivity when evaluating AI investments. Oki Stefanus, Partner at PT Ernst & Young Indonesia, said banks must demonstrate that AI improves lending profitability and controls credit risks, rather than simply cutting costs, to convince boards and investors of its value. Oki Stefanus, Partner at PT Ernst & Young Indonesia “A strong business case is not only about raising the approval rate, but also about proving that credit growth can deliver a better risk-adjusted return than conventional approaches,” he said in an emailed reply to questions. Stefanus said banks should assess AI investments over the medium to long term because benefits might take time as they improve their data, risk models, and operations. Access to alternative credit data alone does not give lenders a lasting advantage, he said. Most banks can obtain information from Indonesia’s credit information system, private credit bureaus, and other sources. The advantage comes from using that information to make better lending decisions, improve risk assessments, and keep loan quality and profitability. Digital banks can experiment faster and make greater use of data, whilst conventional banks have stronger funding, more experience managing risks, and broader customer relationships, Stefanus said. “It is not simply the one with the best technology that will win, but the one that can translate that technology into sustainable growth while keeping asset quality intact,” he added. Stefanus said banks should test AI tools and lending products on a limited scale, with risk management, legal, and compliance teams involved from the start. title: Oobit launches AI payments for stablecoin purchases
excerpt: . Crypto Fintech AI. Oobit launches AI payments for stablecoin purchases. Tue, 13th Oct 2026 (Today). KAREN JOY BACUDO Finance Editor. Oobit has launched AI Payments for supported AI assistants, allowing users to approve purchases funded through their Oobit account with stablecoins. The product launches with assistants including Muse, Grok, Dots, and Instinct. Eligible users in more than 75 countries can connect accounts through a single integration. The system is designed to let an AI assistant complete a specific purchase without gaining ongoing access to a user's account balance or primary payment details. When a user asks an assistant to make a purchase, booking or payment, the assistant prepares the transaction and the user approves it, including a spending limit. Oobit then generates a one-time virtual card for that transaction. The assistant uses the card to complete checkout, while the user's underlying funds and core payment credentials remain outside the assistant's control. How it works. The launch comes as AI assistants move beyond search and recommendation tools into services that can take direct action for consumers. That shift has raised questions about how an assistant can pay for goods or services without being given unrestricted access to a bank card, wallet or account. Oobit's model uses transaction-specific payment credentials rather than a persistent payment method tied to an AI agent. The aim is to reduce the risk of unauthorised spending, overspending and reuse of sensitive payment information by limiting each approval to a single checkout. Funding can come from supported stablecoins and digital assets, including USDT. In some markets, users can also add funds through local payment methods such as bank transfers, mobile money and Pix. "AI can already understand what you want and figure out how to get it. The missing piece is the ability to pay," said Amram Adar, Co-Founder and CEO of Oobit. "That shouldn't depend on where you live or which bank card you have. Whether your money starts as USDT, Pix or mobile money, it should work with AI," Adar said. Control and access. Oobit is positioning the product around user control over authorisation. Under the model, the assistant can request payment approval, but Oobit handles identity, authorisation, and payment execution. That approach reflects a wider debate about how consumer safeguards should operate when software acts on a user's behalf in online commerce. Traditional online payments usually require direct access to a payment card, bank account or digital wallet, but AI-led transactions are creating pressure for more limited, specific permissions. "The question isn't whether AI will be able to make purchases. It's how we make sure people remain in control when it does," Adar said. "An assistant shouldn't need access to your entire wallet just to buy something you've already approved. We're separating the permission to complete a payment from access to the money behind it," he said. Adar described the system as a way to tie one approved purchase to one payment instrument. "If you ask an AI to book a hotel, you want it to complete that booking, not have the ability to spend your money somewhere else tomorrow," he said. "One transaction, one card, and a limit approved by the user. That's the principle behind AI Payments," Adar said. Stablecoin use. The rollout also reflects efforts by digital asset companies to expand the use of stablecoins beyond transfers and direct wallet-to-wallet payments. By linking stablecoin balances to AI-assisted consumer purchases, Oobit aims to place digital assets into more mainstream buying flows. "Stablecoins have already made it possible to move money digitally across borders. The next step is making that money useful in the experiences people actually use," Adar said. title: Woori Bank to Launch AI-Based Fraud Detection System Next Month
excerpt: . | |. View images in original article →. Woori Bank will begin operating a next-generation fraud detection system (FDS) combining artificial intelligence and telecommunications data starting next month to prevent financial fraud. Chung Jin-wan, chief executive of Woori Bank, said preventing financial fraud is the bank's top management priority, speaking at a press briefing at the bank's headquarters in Seoul's Jung-gu district on the 12th. "We will not stop at compensating victims. We will strengthen our preventive framework further by detecting warning signs one step ahead," the CEO said. The bank will activate the next-generation FDS next month. The system aims to block customer losses in advance by using AI to analyze a wide range of fraud patterns and by expanding the scope of data it draws on. Woori Bank also plans to break its fraud response framework into three stages — building the foundation, expanding capabilities and leading prevention — to embed fraud prevention capacity across the entire bank. The bank is overhauling its fraud response framework because fraud techniques are growing more sophisticated alongside advances in AI. Financial fraud losses in South Korea rose to 2. 3755 trillion won (about $1. 65 billion) last year from 791. 1 billion won (about $550 million) in 2022, according to the Korean National Police Agency. That marks a roughly threefold increase in three years. Tracking the crimes has become increasingly difficult as voice phishing rings split their bases across multiple countries, including China, Cambodia and the Philippines. Phishing crimes exploiting the so-called "pig butchering" method have surged recently. Perpetrators communicate with victims over long periods through social media or mobile messengers to build trust before recommending investments. In many cases they start with small amounts, gradually increase the sums and then disappear after receiving a final payment. Jeon Jae-hong, head of Woori Bank's financial fraud prevention department and a financial investigation specialist who spent 24 years with the police, stressed the importance of awareness. "Recognizing that I too could fall victim to financial fraud is more important than anything else," Jeon said. "Woori Bank will become a bank that leads in preventing financial fraud. ". The efforts of Woori Bank, which created a dedicated fraud prevention unit last year, are producing results. Last month the bank detected a pattern in which 290 million won was deposited into a customer account and 30 million won was then transferred to a suspicious account. Based on statements from those involved in the transactions, the bank placed a temporary hold on the account and prevented an additional 260 million won in losses. The bank also filed 83 suspicious transaction reports (STRs) through cooperation between its FDS and anti-money laundering (AML) units. Woori Bank plans to form a financial fraud prevention team staffed by former police officers with experience investigating financial fraud. Visual Briefing NEW. Card News. title: Kakao Bank launches first account for foreign residents, with 5-minute sign-up via chatbot
excerpt: FINANCE Kakao Bank launches first account for foreign residents, with 5-minute sign-up via chatbot. by Yu Hye-rim Published : Oct. 12, 2026 - 10:00:00. Copy Completed!. View Korean Original. Service covers nationals from more than 200 countries. Offers account, card, overseas remittance, AI and lifestyle benefits. Kakao Bank is launching a mobile banking service tailored for foreign residents in South Korea, allowing them to open an account in about five minutes without visiting a branch and send money to roughly 200 countries through the app. The bank unveiled the service Monday at Novotel Ambassador in Dongdaemun-gu, Seoul, at a press event called a "foreigner service press talk," introducing the foreign resident account, a Friends debit card, overseas remittance, multilingual customer support, security features and lifestyle conveniences. The offering is designed to let foreign customers open an account, waive transfer and ATM fees, earn cashback on their debit card, and access AI and lifestyle benefits — all without visiting a branch. The foreign resident account is open to non-Korean nationals aged 19 and older from more than 200 countries, including China and Vietnam. The entire account-opening process runs through a chatbot, and customers who do not require additional screening can complete sign-up in about five minutes. Required documents — such as proof of employment, pay stubs and certificates of residency — can be submitted directly through the app. A selfie verification system designed for foreign users, combined with public MyData, reduces the information customers need to enter and verify manually, including name, nationality, address and occupation. When overseas tax-obligation checks or additional screening are needed, customers can track progress within the app. Until now, foreign customers opening a bank account in Korea have had to submit documents or visit a branch in person for know-your-customer checks and overseas tax-obligation verification. Even when non-face-to-face services were available, the process often could not be completed entirely within an app, and limited foreign-language support created further barriers. Kakao Bank designed the service with those pain points in mind, building the sign-up flow, language options and authentication environment around the needs of foreign users. The bank made it possible to handle everything from account opening to product use and customer inquiries on a mobile device, and added features for issuing certificates needed for visa renewals and checking balances in familiar currencies. Balance certificates and transaction statements needed for visa renewals and other purposes are available through a dedicated document-issuance menu. The account screen displays the won balance alongside real-time conversions in nine currencies. Transfer and ATM deposit and withdrawal fees are waived with no conditions. Foreign customers can also open a group account or sign up for Safe Box, Kakao Bank's parking account. Each customer may hold up to two foreign resident accounts. Card and overseas remittance services are also available. Foreign customers will initially be issued a domestic-use Friends debit card offering the same cashback benefits as those available to Korean customers. A debit card that supports overseas payments is planned for release later this year. Foreign customers can also apply for the Kakao Bank Chakbut Shinhan Card, a private-label credit card developed in partnership with Shinhan Card that launched in August. Sole proprietors can apply for a business-owner affiliated credit card, and a service that lets customers compare benefits across multiple cards before applying is also available. excerpt: . Australia outlines plans to make AI companies prove their safety systems work. By chief digital political correspondent Clare Armstrong. Topic: AI. Posted Thu at 2:19am Thursday at 2:19am Thu 8 Oct 2026 at 2:19am , updated Thu at 6:16am Thursday at 6:16am Thu 8 Oct 2026 at 6:16am. In short:. The federal government wants AI developers to demonstrate their safety systems are effective under proposed laws drawing on banking and aviation regulation. It argues voluntary safeguards are inadequate when companies face intense pressure to develop increasingly powerful technology. What's next?. Labor is finalising national AI standards due by the end of the year with plans to legislate the new rules in 2027. Australia would require AI companies to prove they are properly testing models and preventing harm under proposed new laws modelled on banking and aviation safety rules. The federal government is finalising plans to regulate frontier artificial intelligence through national standards due by the end of the year, with recent incidents involving rogue agents underscoring the risks of the rapidly advancing technology. Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton has signalled the government wants to make AI companies demonstrate their safety systems are effective, rather than dictate how they should manage every risk. He outlined the case for tougher frontier AI oversight in a speech in Sydney today, arguing Australia should put the "burden" where the risk was created. "AI needs regulating because its harms are severe, hard to undo, borne by people who never chose them and sometimes invisible until they arrive," he said. "The market will not fix this alone, because the incentives reward speed and capability, and even the people at the top of the industry cannot slow down by themselves. ". Safety rules for banks, aviation show path for AI. Rather than trying to keep pace with the technology by banning specific dangerous behaviours, Australia's approach would require AI companies continually test for risks and show they can prevent harm. Mr Charlton said there was not enough incentive for companies to comply with "voluntary" regulations or codes when it came to frontier AI risks. "You cannot ask firms to volunteer against their own competitive interest amid a manic race involving trillions of dollars and then be surprised when they do not," he said. He also warned detailed prescriptive rules could end up "out of date before the ink is dry" due to the pace of the technology's development. "For these reasons, there is much that Australia can learn from systems-based regulatory approaches, that puts the onus and accountability on companies for managing how they develop products and services safely," he said. Mr Charlton said this model was already used in workplace health and safety, supervision of banks and aspects of aviation safety. "The goal is to ensure companies are meeting the expectations of safety, without trying to specify every hazard," he said. "The question isn't only 'did something go wrong' but is there a serious system in place to detect risks and prevent incidents occurring. ". Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson said Australia should be "very pragmatic and sensible" about regulating AI, adding he believed the position outlined by Mr Charlton was heading "in the right direction". "The details will matter. We look forward to understanding what the government is proposing exactly," he told Afternoon Briefing. Senator Paterson said the Coalition would not give Labor a "blank cheque" on AI but would support policies that landed in a "sensible place". "The AI opportunity before Australia is a once-in-a-generation opportunity, but it does come with a very real risk, and it is important parties of government act in the national interest and with goodwill to try and get this right on behalf of our country," he said.
